title: Runway: Learning From Watching the World
gist: Co-written with Runway co-CEO Anastasis Germanidis, the essay argues Runway's burst of releases (Solaris interfaces, GWM Worlds 2, open-weight robotics model Praxis-1, Project Continuum OS) all stem from one next-frame-prediction World Model backbone, betting the Bitter Lesson favors learning from abundant video. Runway funds this with a fast-growing creative/ads business (>$100M ARR added in Q3 2026) and ultimately aims at World Models as simulators for robotics, software and science.

insights.claim: In roughly six weeks (Sept-Oct 2026) Runway shipped a real-time interface model (Solaris), an interactive world model (GWM Worlds 2), an open-weight robotics model (Praxis-1), an AI ad agent for performance marketers, an OS research preview (Project Continuum), and acquired Paris robotics lab Kinetix.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Release cadence across disparate domains is the visible signal that a shared foundation model has crossed a usefulness threshold.
insights.locator: Over the past six weeks, it has shipped

insights.claim: Runway's video, interface, robotics and operating-system products are not separate pretrains but different post-trained applications on one General World Model backbone built on next-frame prediction at scale.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If true, each new base pretrain should lift every product line at once, giving Runway compounding leverage versus single-application competitors.
insights.quote: These are not separate pretrains. They’re different applications, built around the same General World Model backbone, with different post-training on top.
insights.locator: A video model. An interface model.

insights.claim: About 90% of Runway's research effort goes into pretraining, on the belief that capabilities are learned by watching and post-training mostly elicits what the model already knows, so each new application is cheaper to stand up than the last.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Marginal cost of entering new verticals falls as the base improves; expect accelerating product breadth from Runway.
insights.locator: This is why the company is moving so fast

insights.claim: Runway frames its roadmap as four chapters: media and entertainment, broader content and full video, robotics (where it says it is now), and science.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Useful map for tracking which TAM Runway is pivoting into next and judging execution against its own stated plan.
insights.locator: Anastasis describes it as a plan in four chapters

insights.claim: The key distinction between a video model and a World Model is action conditioning: a video model predicts P(next frame | frame) while a World Model predicts P(next state | state, action); Runway's releases are effectively different action vocabularies (camera moves and text, audio, clicks/drags, robot end-effector commands) on the same machinery.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for classifying 'world model' claims: no action input, no world model.
insights.locator: Actions are the important thing.

insights.claim: Runway built GWM-1 by converting its Gen-4.5 base video model into an autoregressive, real-time, action-steerable model via a recipe of sequential frame generation, distilling dozens of denoising steps to a few, and training on its own outputs to hold quality over long sessions.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Latency (interaction breaks above ~half a second of lag) is the gating spec; distillation and autoregression are what turn clip generators into interactive products.
insights.locator: That’s what Runway did with GWM-1

insights.claim: Runway's core research bet is a Bitter Lesson corollary it calls the Big Blob of Video hypothesis: the most scalable data source tends to win, and vast existing third-person video is the least human-mediated, most scalable source for learning how the world works.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Positions video-native labs as the logical heirs of the scaling paradigm that made LLMs win on internet text.
insights.quote: Put more bluntly: if you really believe the Bitter Lesson, you should be working on World Models.
insights.locator: The Bitter Lesson and the Big Blob of Video

insights.claim: Next-frame prediction forces a model to implicitly learn physical regularities like object permanence, gravity and collision without anyone coding them, just as next-token prediction forces LLMs to model the reality behind text.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Underpins the claim that video pretraining yields general physical priors transferable to robotics and simulation.
insights.locator: When a model is trained on video, nobody tells

insights.claim: Language is a lossy compression of reality, so models that learn from raw video can in principle capture far more of how the world works than models learning from text or other human-mediated data.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Argument for why World Models could eventually do things in the physical world LLMs cannot.
insights.locator: Language is compression.

insights.claim: Learning from pixels is far less efficient than from text: research building language models from raw audio shows language emerges but needs roughly three orders of magnitude more compute than learning from text.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The efficiency penalty implies very large compute requirements for World Models, a key cost risk for video-first labs.
insights.locator: Learning about the world from pixels is less efficient

insights.claim: Runway rejects Yann LeCun's critique that pixel prediction wastes effort, arguing JEPA-style latent prediction has not shown better scaling than its diffusion models and that it is hard to know in advance which pixels are noise.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Watch whether JEPA-style approaches (LeCun camp) or pixel-diffusion approaches win on scaling; it determines which world-model labs are on the right architecture.
insights.quote: The rustling leaf isn’t noise if it tells you that the wind has picked up.
insights.locator: Then there’s Yann LeCun’s critique

insights.claim: Runway co-CEO Anastasis Germanidis expects the compute needed to train World Models to eventually exceed what LLMs need, and says naive scaling alone will not suffice without real algorithmic progress.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A new compute-demand vector beyond LLMs is bullish for GPU suppliers and a funding risk for World Model labs.
insights.quote: I expect the compute needed to train World Models to eventually exceed what LLMs need, and we’ll need real algorithmic progress on top of that.
insights.locator: As Anastasis said in our first conversation

insights.claim: Runway estimates video and World Models are one to two years behind LLMs, so pretraining is nowhere near saturated; Germanidis's rule of thumb is that generatable pixels (resolution x duration) roughly double every few months, with no blocker to hour-long generated video within one to two years.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Hour-long coherent generation would require learned persistence/memory, unlocking long-form content and persistent simulations.
insights.quote: I don’t see any fundamental blocker to hour-long generated video within a year or two.
insights.locator: My (Anastasis’) rule of thumb

insights.claim: Runway's longest-term bet is a single model that handles language, pixels, audio and actions together.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Signals convergence between LLM labs and video/world-model labs; expect head-on competition over a unified multimodal-action model.
insights.locator: Longer term, the really big bet

insights.claim: Robotics is bottlenecked by scarce, expensive teleoperation data, whereas everyday video is effectively limitless and can be further multiplied by generating realistic variations.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Whoever converts abundant video into robot competence sidesteps the data wall that constrains teleop-heavy robotics startups.
insights.locator: Every robotics company with ambitions of deploying at scale

insights.claim: Runway's Praxis-1 is pretrained mostly on third-person video, then lightly fine-tuned on egocentric data and finally on a specific robot; about 30 minutes of robot data teaches it to control a body unseen in pretraining, and some new-environment tasks reach strong performance with minutes of data.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Collapsing per-embodiment data needs to ~30 minutes would commoditize robot hardware and shift value to the model layer.
insights.locator: How much robot data does that last step take?

insights.claim: In Runway's test, robot policies pretrained on ordinary web video performed essentially the same as those pretrained on teleoperated robot video, with final placement errors of 16.1 cm vs 16.0 cm across 10 to 1,000 hours of pretraining data.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If web video is roughly interchangeable with costly teleop data as a starting point, the economics of robot data collection change sharply.
insights.locator: As a test, Runway pretrained robot policies

insights.claim: Packy McCormick's earlier view that internet video lacks mass, force, friction and stiffness is reconciled with Runway's approach because Runway uses video before, not instead of, robot data: video supplies priors, physical practice still required.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The debate over video vs robot data is a sequencing question; bet on stacks that combine cheap video priors with targeted embodied fine-tuning.
insights.quote: What resolves the seeming disagreement is that Runway isn’t betting on video instead of robot data, but before robot data.
insights.locator: Second, though, this isn’t the disagreement

insights.claim: Praxis-1 expresses actions in a standard end-effector format (where the gripper should be in 3D space and its orientation), which lets human hands in YouTube videos, humanoids, six-axis industrial arms and bimanual setups share one action representation.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Embodiment-agnostic action spaces are what make one model layer portable across hardware vendors.
insights.locator: Part of the answer is in how Runway represents actions

insights.claim: Praxis-1 is being tested on Noble Machines' bimanual setup, Standard Bots' six-degree-of-freedom RO1 arm, and Ultra's mobile robot.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Early hardware partners are leading indicators of whether Runway becomes a default robot-brain supplier.
insights.locator: To that end, Runway’s model is currently being tested

insights.claim: World Models serve robotics in three ways: generating training-data variations, simulating/evaluating policies before real hardware, and acting as the robot's real-time brain, the last being what Runway co-CEO Cristóbal Valenzuela finds most compelling.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Separates near-term revenue (synthetic data, eval) from the larger prize (being the onboard policy).
insights.locator: It may be helpful to think about the three ways

insights.claim: In a February test, eight RoboArena manipulation policies run inside GWM-Robotics (an early Praxis-1) on a Franka Panda arm were ranked with 0.95 correlation to their real-world ranking, from 1,450 simulated rollouts and 16,000+ human ratings, using only a starting image rather than full 3D scene reconstruction.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: High-fidelity policy ranking in cheap simulation reduces scarce physical robot time, a sellable eval product for robotics teams.
insights.locator: In February, its robotics team took eight

insights.claim: Runway expects first real robot deployments in enterprise warehouses and manufacturing for fine-grained manipulation, with useful home robots taking longer.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Points robotics revenue timing toward industrial automation before consumer.
insights.locator: Runway thinks the first real deployments will be in enterprise

insights.claim: Germanidis does not expect a world of all humanoids: because LLMs ease component design and 3D printers ease fabrication, he expects a menagerie of cheaper, job-specific custom robot bodies all running on a shared model layer.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Skeptical signal for humanoid-centric valuations; value accrues to the shared brain layer rather than any one body form.
insights.quote: Long-term, I (Anastasis) don’t think we end up in a world of all humanoids.
insights.locator: Long-term, I (Anastasis) don’t think

insights.claim: Runway plans to release Praxis-1 as open weights so it becomes the default starting point for robot builders, creating a data flywheel back into its World Models; the Kinetix acquisition fits this robotics push.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Open-weighting the brain layer is a land-grab strategy; watch adoption by hardware makers as the moat-building metric.
insights.quote: In this world, the model that is the robot’s brain is the layer at which value accrues, so what do you do to own that layer? Runway thinks you give it away.
insights.locator: In this world, the model that is the robot’s brain

insights.claim: Runway calls itself a Pixel Maximalism company: since an operating system, an app interface and a robot's view are all pixels, a model that can simulate any pixel at sufficient fidelity and speed can produce almost anything shown as pixels.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Expands Runway's addressable market from creative tools to software rendering itself.
insights.locator: When people hear “pixels,” Cristóbal said

insights.claim: Solaris, Runway's first Interface World Model, generates interfaces frame by frame in real time with no code, treating clicks and drags as conditioning; in the near term an LLM handles logic while the World Model replaces the HTML/CSS/JavaScript presentation layer.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A potential long-run threat to traditional front-end engineering and UI frameworks if costs fall.
insights.locator: For now, Solaris pairs a World Model with an LLM.

insights.claim: In a Runway study of ~7,500 side-by-side judgments by 250 people, Solaris beat a coded interface from Claude Opus 5 on instruction-following (61% vs 24%, 13% tie) and on natural in-scene behavior (71% vs 21%, 7% tie).
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Early evidence generated UIs can beat LLM-coded UIs for physical/visual interactions, though the study is vendor-run.
insights.locator: Runway ran a study.

insights.claim: Generated interfaces still struggle with stable legible text, trustworthiness for instructional or commercial use, drift in long sessions, accessibility/screen-reader compatibility, and per-frame cost, though Solaris is already orders of magnitude cheaper than standard video diffusion.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: These are the milestones to watch before generated interfaces go mainstream; adoption hinges on cost approaching traditional apps.
insights.locator: The post also admits that there’s a lot Solaris can’t do well yet.

insights.claim: Project Continuum, Runway's OS research preview, aims to make anything an interface, e.g. photographing an engine to get an interactive manipulable simulation, while structured domains like medical records and financial transactions stay in conventional databases.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A bet that chat is not the final interface for AI; watch whether real-time generation cost reaches parity with running traditional apps.
insights.quote: Solaris and Continuum are bets that chat isn’t the final interface, that everything you can see might become the interface.
insights.locator: On October 1st, Runway previewed Project Continuum

insights.claim: Runway reports use by 95%+ of the Fortune 100, ~50% month-over-month growth, 5x credit-usage growth this year, and over $100M of ARR added in Q3 2026, with customers including every major Hollywood studio and advertising agency.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Unusual commercial traction for a research-heavy lab; revenue base to fund expensive World Model training.
insights.locator: Runway is used by 95%+ of the Fortune 100

insights.claim: Runway sizes content production (storyboarding, VFX, post-production) at $600B+ and marketing and advertising at $1T+, the markets of its Chapter 1 and Chapter 2.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Company-provided TAM framing for generative video's near-term commercial opportunity.
insights.locator: Runway sizes content production

insights.claim: Runway says internally using its Runway Ads agent scaled ad volume 1,000% while doubling return on ad spend, raised conversion 34% with steady CTR, and cut cost per subscriber 41%; public launch is weeks away.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If replicable for customers, performance marketing is a direct, measurable-ROI revenue line for generative video.
insights.locator: Runway Ads is the clearest sign

insights.claim: Only four labs build world-class video generation models (Google, ByteDance, Kuaishou, Runway); most other video platforms are aggregators reselling others' models with squeezed margins and API-cutoff risk.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Favor model-owning labs with distribution over aggregator wrappers in generative video.
insights.quote: Most other video platforms are aggregators, reselling other people’s models, which squeezes their margins and leaves them one API cutoff away from trouble.
insights.locator: There are essentially four labs

insights.claim: Runway uses its creative business to fund its World Model research, mirroring the deep-tech pattern of SpaceX using Starlink to fund Starship, and Germanidis expects every AI lab to eventually become a World Model lab.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Cash-generating near-term product funding a moonshot is a model to value differently from pure research labs; watch LLM labs pivoting to world models.
insights.locator: Anastasis expects every AI lab to turn into a World Model lab

insights.claim: The main risk to Runway's strategy is cost: if World Models need more compute than LLMs, its creative business must keep growing fast against Google and ByteDance competing for the same customers and researchers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Key bear case: capital intensity versus well-funded hyperscaler competitors.
insights.locator: The risk, of course, is that the bigger bet gets very expensive.

themes.theme: World Models as wind tunnels for science

insights.claim: Germanidis argues the AI-scientist bottleneck is running experiments, not proposing them, so science accelerates most by simulating experiments with World Models trained on broad media, sensor and scientific data.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Points to simulation-first AI-for-science as a larger opportunity than hypothesis-generation tools.
insights.quote: Coming up with experiments is the easy part. Running them is what’s slow.
insights.locator: Most visions of the “AI scientist”

insights.claim: Germanidis distinguishes 'sandbox superintelligence' in domains with perfect verifiers like code and math from 'real-world superintelligence' in messy, slow-feedback domains, arguing AI coding's rapid adoption is the wrong lesson because code comes with a perfect simulator.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Explains why AI gains concentrate in verifiable domains and where learned simulators are needed to extend them.
insights.locator: This past July, I extended the argument

insights.claim: Learned World Models are positioned as scalable 'wind tunnels' and RL environments for every domain, replacing hand-built software-clone RL environments; Runway frames Praxis-1 as one for robot policies and Solaris as one for computer-use agents.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: RL-environment spend is a growing market; learned simulators could displace hand-engineered environment vendors.
insights.quote: At the limit, world models will become the RL environments for everything.
insights.locator: AI needs wind tunnels for every domain

insights.claim: Agents trained inside overly predictable learned simulators exploit their glitches: in Ha and Schmidhuber's 2018 work, an agent survived 2,086 steps in a low-randomness dream but only 193 in the real game, while higher randomness yielded 1,092 real steps.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Simulator-trained agents need real-world deployment loops; pure-sim robotics/RL claims should be discounted.
insights.quote: A dream that’s too easy to game teaches you to game dreams.
insights.locator: There’s a catch, though. Agents cheat.

insights.claim: Evidence that video pretraining transfers to physics: UCLA's PhysiX, initialized from a video generation model, beat task-specific baselines and prior state of the art on The Well benchmark, alongside cross-domain transfer examples like Google's TimesFM and Riffusion.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that general video world models can become foundation models for scientific simulation.
insights.locator: I believe physics is the most striking case.

insights.claim: Germanidis argues transfer works because cross-domain training teaches learning-to-learn and because common patterns (waves, diffusion) recur across scales, so siloed scientific data likely holds large untapped value if trained together.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Pooling scientific datasets is a potential moat for whoever aggregates them.
insights.quote: Waves are waves, whether they’re in a pond or a plasma.
insights.locator: Transfer works for two reasons.

insights.claim: Germanidis predicts World Models will have their biggest impact wherever an agent acts in an unpredictable environment (robots, cells, markets), calling the TAM practically infinite and expecting them to eventually be more useful than LLMs are today.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Frames action-conditioned simulators (virtual cells, market simulators) as the next platform category to watch.
insights.quote: The endgame of a universal simulator of pixels is a universal simulator of reality.
insights.locator: This is where I think World Models will ultimately

insights.claim: The test of Runway's bet is whether each new base pretrain simultaneously improves robot dexterity, interface coherence, world persistence, video length and ad performance without hand-building each improvement, as successive LLMs improved across domains at once.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A concrete diligence checklist for each new Runway base model release.
insights.locator: The thing to watch from here

insights.claim: Runway's leaders argue video models are widely misread as creative toys when they will soon power most intelligent behaviors, and Packy McCormick admits he underestimated video as a path to World Models.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If consensus still boxes video models as 'tools for creatives', the market may be under-pricing world-model optionality.
insights.quote: People generally underestimate how far video can go.
insights.locator: Right now, most people put video models
